title: Traceable Quantum Secret Sharing
authors: Mengyan Qiao, Jian Long, Yu Li, Zhu Cao
abstract: Quantum secret sharing protects distributed quantum information against unauthorized reconstruction, yet existing schemes provide no intrinsic accountability when shares are leaked or forged. This missing capability is particularly relevant in realistic distributed settings, where compromised participants may either expose valid shares or maliciously interfere with reconstruction. Here we establish a framework for traceable quantum secret sharing under these two threat models. We introduce leakage-verifiable and traceable quantum secret sharing (LVT-QSS), which attributes leaked shares through an explicit leakage verification mechanism, and malicious-traceable and accountable quantum secret sharing (MTA-QSS), which identifies participants who submit forged shares during reconstruction. We formulate security definitions for both settings and prove that the proposed protocols satisfy the corresponding guarantees against the relevant adversaries. Numerical simulations under per-share depolarizing noise further quantify the robustness of the proposed schemes and identify verification as the dominant noise sensitive stage. These results incorporate accountability into quantum secret sharing and provide a foundation for traceable distributed quantum cryptography.
summary: This paper develops frameworks for traceable and accountable Quantum Secret Sharing (QSS) to address the lack of accountability when shares are leaked or forged. It introduces LVT-QSS and MTA-QSS, providing rigorous security proofs for both leakage-verifiable and malicious-traceable scenarios. The work advances distributed quantum cryptography by embedding accountability into the core security guarantees.
main_problem: Existing Quantum Secret Sharing (QSS) schemes lack intrinsic accountability mechanisms to track leaked or forged shares, which is critical in realistic distributed quantum settings.
main_result: The authors introduce and prove the security of two schemes: LVT-QSS (for leaked shares) and MTA-QSS (for forged shares), successfully incorporating accountability into QSS.
method: The work involves formulating rigorous security definitions for both leakage and malicious behavior, followed by cryptographic proofs demonstrating that the proposed protocols satisfy these guarantees.
model_or_system: The model is a threshold quantum secret sharing scheme protecting a quantum state $|\psiangle$ across $n$ participants. It relies on quantum information theory concepts, including CPTP maps, and cryptographic primitives like post-quantum symmetric-key encryption and quantum-secure hash functions.
key_observables: Traceability advantage ($	ext{Adv}_{	ext{trace}}$), distinguishing advantage for secrecy ($	ext{Adv}_{	ext{secrecy}}$), and non-imputability advantage ($	ext{Adv}_{	ext{ni}}$).
important_parameters: Threshold parameters ($k, m$), noise model (per-share depolarizing noise), and the security parameter $\lambda$.
main_assumptions: The security proofs rely heavily on the underlying cryptographic hash function ($H$) being quantum-secure collision resistant and preimage resistant.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem gap in QSS accountability. It then details the LVT-QSS scheme, proving its tracer secrecy and traceability. Subsequently, it analyzes the MTA-QSS scheme, proving its security properties, and concludes by comparing the robustness of both protocols.
why_interesting: While the focus is on quantum cryptography, the rigorous security proofs involving quantum channels and information leakage are fundamental theoretical tools applicable to analyzing decoherence and information flow in complex quantum systems.
